extracted.intended_audience: the people of the State of New York; American citizens and voters considering adoption of the proposed Constitution (delegates, informed public)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for assessing whether a confederation or proposed national Constitution can preserve the Union and perform essential government functions. Focuses on institutional powers, modes of enforcement, and the proper allocation of national vs state responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of Union to your political safety and happiness (the sacred knot which binds the people of America together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union is presented as essential to avoid 'complication of dangers' (anarchy, loss of respect abroad, decay of commerce, public credit). The essay argues citizens should prioritize preservation of the Union and reject proposals that would sever it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must have sufficient energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of the United States is destitute of energy under the present Confederation; a national government must possess 'energy' to discharge its duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of insufficient energy includes lack of troops, treasury, or capacity to enforce treaties, declining public credit, depressed commerce, and inability of ambassadors to be treated as real representatives. A competent national system must remedy these defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid legislation aimed only at States (legislate for individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation is the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS, in their CORPORATE or COLLECTIVE CAPACITIES, as contradistinguished from the INDIVIDUALS of which they consist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A workable federal government must 'carry its agency to the persons of the citizens' — i.e., extend authority to individuals so laws operate immediately on citizens rather than as mere recommendations to state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law requires sanction enforceable against individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Government implies the power of making laws; it is essential that laws be attended with a sanction — a penalty or punishment for disobedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can be applied by (1) courts and ministers of justice (coercion of the magistracy) directed at individuals, or (2) military force directed at collective bodies. The preferred and practical mode for ordinary government is enforcement via the ordinary magistracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution of national laws must not depend on state legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: If execution of the laws of the national government requires intervention of the State legislatures, those particular governments can interrupt progress by inaction or evasive acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws that need state cooperation can be defeated by 'NOT TO ACT, or to ACT EVASIVELY' without obvious alarm. Direct operation upon citizens prevents surreptitious evasion and makes interruptions obvious and legally contestable.

rubrics_metrics.name: A national government that can only enforce by military coercion is impracticable and dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: If the national government cannot operate upon individuals it would require military force to enforce laws against states — a scheme that would degenerate into a military despotism and is impracticable given resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military enforcement would likely produce civil war or at least dependence on a large standing army; the Union lacks resources to maintain such an army, and use of force against members would invite alliances, foreign meddling, and dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government must be able to raise men and money directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Confederation, the United States can make requisitions for men and money but lacks authority to raise them by regulations extending to individual citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A true government must have the power to raise troops and public revenue directly from individuals rather than relying on state discretion, because state noncompliance has repeatedly frustrated requisitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish a league (treaty) from a government by enforceable, person-directed powers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing absurd in a league of independent nations for defined purposes, but such compacts depend on good faith and lack the sanctions and execution mechanisms of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be a government (not merely a league) the Union must include 'ingredients' that make it different from a treaty — i.e., powers that operate on persons with sanctions and institutional channels of enforcement rather than mere promises between sovereignties.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'legislation for states' principle is the parent of anarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of legislation for sovereign States, supported by military coercion, has been shown in history to be the parent of anarchy and often leads to civil war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical confederacies that limited national coercion to states have failed in proportion to that principle's prevalence; reliance on force against states tends to produce violent dissolution rather than compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical division of powers: national vs local subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects like commerce, finance, negotiation, and war belong to national authority; domestic police, ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice, agriculture and similar local concerns belong to State governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The national government should be entrusted with matters that have charms for ambition (commerce, finance, war) while local administrations retain the immediate, visible functions (criminal/civil justice) that secure popular attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments provide vital counterbalance through ordinary justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice by State governments is 'the most powerful, most universal, and most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaining local justice in state hands is a natural and beneficial counterpoise to national authority; it builds public attachment and helps preserve liberty while national authority handles broader concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compliance tends to spread by example and self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: When some States fail to comply with federal requisitions, others use that as a pretext to withdraw their support; inequalities in compliance produce a chain reaction undermining the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of federal powers must anticipate and prevent contagion of noncompliance (e.g., by giving the Union mechanisms to operate directly on individuals), since selfish calculations (why bear more than others?) will otherwise erode cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective federal authority must be manifest through courts and ordinary magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The majesty of the national authority must be manifested through the medium of the courts of justice; the government must be able to address itself immediately to the hopes and fears of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and ordinary magistrates enable national laws to be enforced without recourse to military coercion; a constitution and enlightened people (and impartial judges) provide checks against unlawful state encroachments.
